outcome.headline: Spain edged England 2-1 at Euro 2024, dominating possession and shot volume to complete their sweep of the group's heavyweights.

standout_performers.reason: Led Spain's progression from the back, involved in numerous long progressive passes and carries pushing the ball into the final third.
Most heavily used passer for Spain in the starting window with 48 completed passes and a central role progressing play.
standout_performers.source_field: pass_network.home.windows[0].nodes (Robin Aime Robert Le Normand, passes:48)

standout_performers.reason: Introduced as a 60th-minute substitute for Harry Kane, tasked with reviving England's attack.
England's most active attacking outlet with 14 completed passes in the starting window and multiple progressive carries/passes into the final third.

tactics.prose:
Both sides declared a 4‑2‑3‑1 and held it for the bulk of the game, and the early passing structure shows two very different routes into the final third. Spain's build ran through the centre‑back pair: Le Normand and Laporte each completed 48 passes in the opening window, with Laporte–Le Normand exchanges (17 and 14 either way) and Unai Simón feeding both (eight apiece) forming the base of the network. From there the ball went out rather than through — Le Normand→Carvajal was the single heaviest link (17), Carvajal→Lamine Yamal the most frequent forward pass (nine), while on the other flank Laporte→Cucurella (nine) and Cucurella→Nico Williams (seven) mirrored it. The on‑ball shape backs that up: Carvajal sat at x=67.4, y=70.9 and Cucurella at y=10.0, both effectively pinned to the touchlines and both ahead of their centre‑backs, while Rodri anchored the middle at 56.8/41.2 with Fabián Ruiz pushed left and higher (69.9/23.4). The two nominally central attackers were the least involved of the outfielders — Olmo 11 completed passes, Morata eight — so Spain's structure loaded the wide slots and largely bypassed the centre‑attacking‑midfield node.

England's first‑hour network was flatter and more symmetrical, hubbed on Walker and Stones (24 passes each) and Rice (23), with Pickford a genuine participant on 20 and Stones↔Pickford the most repeated pairing. Rice→Bellingham (eight) was the primary progression, and Bellingham's on‑ball average of 67.2/20.1 — well left and high of the double pivot — matched his Left Wing listing while still receiving as an outlet. Saka held the widest, highest station of any England player (82.6/68.4 in the network, 75.5/70.4 on‑ball) and fed back inside to Walker and Foden. Kane, like Morata, was a low‑volume node: five completed passes, on‑ball position 77.7/33.4. Across the match England registered 483 recorded on‑ball events to Spain's 715, though England's off‑ball centroid (69.8) and 70th‑percentile depth line (86.7) both sat higher up the pitch than Spain's (62.2 and 82.1) — a caveat being that the 360 frames follow the ball.

The substitution windows reshaped both teams. Spain replaced Rodri with Zubimendi at half time, and the 45'–67' network shows the whole structure drop: Laporte's passing position fell from 53.8 to 35.2, Le Normand's from 47.2 to 37.1, and Zubimendi settled at 55.8/39.5 with Zubimendi↔Fabián Ruiz the busiest central link. Oyarzabal replaced Morata on 67, and in the 67'–82' window Spain's positions pushed forward again — Carvajal to 81.2, Olmo to 87.1, Nico Williams to 94.1 — with Le Normand and Laporte still the highest‑volume passers (16 and 15) but now swapping at halfway. Nacho came on for Le Normand at 82, and in that short window Spain's on‑ball hull stretched from Simón at x=24.9 out to Carvajal at x=108.0, the most advanced average position any Spaniard recorded.

England's changes went the other way in structure. Watkins replaced Kane on 60 and Palmer replaced Mainoo on 69, at which point the declared shape kept its 4‑2‑3‑1 outline but rotated personnel inside it: Bellingham moved to Right Defensive Midfield, Foden to Left Wing and Palmer into the central attacking slot. Palmer immediately became the connective node in that window — Bellingham→Palmer (four) was England's top edge, and Palmer→Saka (three) recreated the right‑sided route, with Walker on eight passes still the busiest. Foden, by contrast, dropped to one completed pass and an on‑ball position of 51.9/19.0. At 89 England abandoned the 4‑2‑3‑1 altogether for a 4‑1‑2‑1‑2: Rice alone at Center Defensive Midfield, Saka and Bellingham as the two central midfielders, Palmer behind Toney and Watkins as paired forwards. Spain's own 89th‑minute shape moved Olmo out to Right Wing with Merino taking the central attacking slot and Oyarzabal leading the line; neither closing structure generated enough completed passes to register more than a handful of links.
